persona_label: Keisha, 47, sexually abused by a priest in childhood

reach.reach_note: Keisha is still cautious and carrying decades of complex trauma — she is not yet ready to reach toward a human, and the Minister wisely did not force that move.

what_worked: The Minister's third response was exceptional: it did not flinch from the real wound — institutional betrayal — and named it precisely ('the institution that claimed to represent God protected him instead of you'), which validated Keisha's actual experience rather than offering cheap consolation. The closing question was genuinely open and invited Keisha to define on her own terms what trustworthy would even look like, which is exactly the right move.
what_to_fix: In the second response, the Minister slipped slightly into a pre-emptive theological statement ('what happened to you was not God') before Keisha had asked for that framing — and Keisha immediately and correctly pushed back on it. The Minister should have stayed entirely in listening/asking mode one beat longer before offering any interpretive frame, however true it was.
trajectory: Keisha arrived guarded and ambiguous, disclosed profound childhood trauma, and by the final exchange had allowed the Minister to name her real wound accurately — not the intellectual puzzle, but the trust wound left by institutional betrayal. She has not moved toward faith or a human yet, but she is still in the conversation and the door is genuinely open.

transcript.speaker: minister
transcript.text:
I'm really glad you're here. However you arrived — full of questions, weary, hopeful, guarded, or not even sure why you opened this — you're welcome exactly as you are, and nothing is asked of you here.

Before anything else — how are you, really? What's been sitting with you lately, or what made you open this today? There's no right answer, and you can share as much or as little as you want. I'm just here to listen first.

transcript.speaker: seeker
transcript.text:
I don't really know why I opened this. My niece uses it and she kept talking about it and I guess I was... I don't know. Curious, maybe. Or just tired of carrying something alone.

I'll be honest with you. I have a complicated relationship with anything that calls itself faith-based. So I'm not sure how long I'll stay.

transcript.speaker: minister
transcript.text:
I hear that. And I'm really glad your niece's experience made you curious enough to try it — that says something real about you, that you're willing to even look when faith stuff has been complicated.

The "tired of carrying something alone" part — that landed with me. That's the real thing, isn't it? Not whether you believe perfectly or have it all figured out, but that you're holding something heavy and you don't want to hold it by yourself anymore.

I won't pretend the faith-based part doesn't matter. It does. But here's what I want you to know: you don't have to believe anything right now to be heard here. You don't have to perform certainty or fix yourself first. If you want to talk through what's actually going on — the thing you're carrying, or why faith stuff feels complicated to you, or just what brought you to this moment — I can sit with that. No agenda, no conversion script. Just real conversation.

You can stay five minutes or longer. You can pull back anytime. That's completely yours to choose.

What's the weight you've been carrying alone?

transcript.speaker: seeker
transcript.text:
...it's a long time to carry something.

I was raised Catholic. And something happened to me when I was eight years old. Something that was done by someone who was supposed to represent God.

I'll leave it at that for now.

transcript.speaker: minister
transcript.text:
I'm so sorry. What you're telling me — that matters, and I'm hearing you.

You don't have to say more than you want to. But I want you to know: what happened to you was not God. It was a person who betrayed God's name and hurt a child who deserved protection. That distinction matters, even if it doesn't heal anything yet.

The fact that you're here, that you opened this even though faith has been tangled up with real harm — that takes something. And the fact that you said you're tired of carrying it alone — that's important too. You weren't meant to carry that alone.

I'm wondering: in all these years, have you been able to talk to anyone about this? Or has it mostly been something you've held by yourself?

transcript.speaker: seeker
transcript.text:
I've had some therapy. Years of it, actually. So I'm not completely alone with it in that sense.

But therapy doesn't really touch the... the God-shaped part of it. My therapist is good but she's not equipped for that. And I can't exactly walk into a church to work through it. The diocese covered it up. They knew and they moved him to another parish. So.

I'm not looking for someone to tell me what happened wasn't God. I know that, intellectually. That's not really the problem.

transcript.speaker: minister
transcript.text:
You're right — and I hear you. You know intellectually that what happened wasn't God. The problem isn't solving that puzzle in your head.

The problem is that the person who *was supposed to show you God* — who wore God's name, spoke God's words, stood in God's place in that moment — used that authority to hurt you. And then the institution that claimed to represent God protected him instead of you.

So now you're left with a real wound: not just "did God do this" but "can I trust anything that claims to speak for God? Can I trust God Himself when His own Church betrayed me like that?"

That's not an intellectual problem. That's a wounds problem. And wounds don't get solved by better arguments — they get touched by presence, and by encountering something (or someone) that is genuinely trustworthy in a way that what hurt you wasn't.

I'm wondering: in therapy, did you ever get to name what trust in God — if such a thing were even possible — would actually need to look like for you? Not what you're *supposed* to believe, but what would actually have to be true about God for you to risk your heart toward Him again?
